questions.q: What is the specific charge of a proton? (charge \(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\), mass \(1.67 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}\))
questions.solution: Specific charge is charge divided by mass: \(\frac{1.60 \times 10^{-19}}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}} = 9.6 \times 10^{7}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}\). The electron's is far larger because its mass is so much smaller.

questions.q: How many neutrons are in a nucleus of carbon-14, \({}^{14}_{6}\text{C}\)?
questions.solution: The nucleon number, 14, counts protons and neutrons together. The proton number is 6. Number of neutrons = 14 − 6 = 8.

questions.q: What are isotopes of an element?

options.A: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
options.B: Atoms with the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons.
options.C: Atoms with the same nucleon number but different proton numbers.
options.D: Atoms with different numbers of electrons.

questions.solution: Isotopes are atoms of the same element, so they have the same proton number. They differ in the number of neutrons, and so in nucleon number. Atoms with different numbers of electrons are ions.

questions.q: Which describes the strong nuclear force between two nucleons?

options.C: Attractive at very short range and repulsive at a few femtometres.
options.D: Repulsive at very short range, attractive up to a few femtometres, and negligible beyond that.

questions.solution: The strong force holds the nucleus together against the repulsion between protons, so it must be attractive at nucleon separations of a few femtometres. At very short range it becomes repulsive, which stops the nucleus collapsing. It has a very short range and is negligible beyond a few femtometres.

questions.q: In the alpha particle scattering experiment, a very small number of alpha particles were deflected through more than 90°. What did this show?

options.A: Most of the atom is empty space.
options.B: The atom contains a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.
options.C: Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed shells.

questions.solution: Only a very strong force could turn an alpha particle back, so the positive charge and nearly all the mass must be concentrated in a tiny nucleus. That so few were deflected shows the nucleus is very small; that most went straight through shows the atom is mostly empty space.

questions.q: In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Which other particle is emitted?
questions.solution: Lepton number must be conserved. It is zero before the decay. The electron has lepton number +1, so the other particle must have −1: an electron antineutrino. The antineutrino also carries away some of the energy, which explains why the electrons have a range of energies.

questions.q: How does an antiparticle compare with its particle?

options.A: The same charge and a smaller mass.
options.B: The opposite charge and a larger mass.
options.C: The same charge and the same mass.
options.D: The opposite charge and the same mass.

questions.solution: A particle and its antiparticle have the same mass and rest energy, but opposite charge (and opposite baryon or lepton number). The positron, for example, has the mass of an electron and a charge of +e.

questions.q: A photon creates an electron and a positron by pair production. The rest energy of an electron is 0.51 MeV. What is the minimum energy of the photon?
questions.solution: The photon must supply the rest energy of both particles, and the positron has the same rest energy as the electron. Minimum energy = 2 × 0.51 = 1.02 MeV. Any extra becomes kinetic energy of the pair.

questions.q: When an electron and a positron at rest annihilate, two photons are produced, not one. Why?

options.C: So that lepton number is conserved.
options.D: Because one photon cannot carry enough energy.

questions.solution: The total momentum before annihilation is zero. A single photon always has momentum, so one photon alone could not conserve it. Two photons of equal energy moving in opposite directions have a total momentum of zero.

questions.q: Which is the exchange particle of the weak interaction?
questions.solution: The weak interaction is carried by W bosons (W⁺ and W⁻). The virtual photon carries the electromagnetic force, and gluons (or pions, between nucleons) carry the strong force.

questions.q: Which statement about mesons is correct?

options.A: They are made of three quarks.
options.C: They do not feel the strong interaction.
options.D: They are made of a quark and an antiquark.

questions.solution: Hadrons are particles made of quarks, which feel the strong interaction. Mesons are hadrons made of one quark and one antiquark; baryons are made of three quarks. Leptons are the fundamental particles that do not feel the strong interaction.

questions.q: What is the quark composition of a proton?
questions.solution: A proton is a baryon made of two up quarks and one down quark. The charges add to +1: two lots of \(+\frac{2}{3}e\) and one of \(-\frac{1}{3}e\). Up, down, down is a neutron.

questions.q: What happens to the quarks in a neutron during beta-minus decay?

options.A: An up quark changes into a down quark.
options.B: An up quark changes into a strange quark.
options.C: A down quark changes into an up quark.
options.D: A down quark changes into an antiup quark.

questions.solution: A neutron (up, down, down) becomes a proton (up, up, down), so one down quark has changed into an up quark. This happens through the weak interaction, with a W⁻ boson that decays into the electron and the antineutrino.

questions.q: Which quantity is not always conserved in particle interactions?
questions.solution: Charge, baryon number, lepton number, energy and momentum are conserved in every interaction. Strangeness is conserved in strong interactions but can change by one in weak interactions, which is how strange particles decay.

questions.q: Which of these particles is a lepton?
questions.solution: Leptons are fundamental particles that do not feel the strong interaction: electrons, muons, neutrinos and their antiparticles. Pions and kaons are mesons, and the neutron is a baryon; all three are hadrons, made of quarks.

questions.q: A proton with momentum \(3.2 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\) moves at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.50 T. What is the radius of its circular path? (charge of a proton \(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
questions.solution: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, which gives \(r = \frac{p}{BQ}\). So \(r = \frac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{0.50 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}}\) = 4.0 m.
